title: the thing that's yours to do
hook: a warrior puts down his bow and says he no longer knows what's right
carry: do the thing that's yours to do

segments.voice: Yesterday, om: three sounds and a silence. Your line was one sound, before words. Did you take that one breath before speaking? Two words on your strand now. Day three.

On a field called Kurukshetra, two armies face each other. Conch shells blast. Banners go up. And a warrior named Arjuna asks his charioteer to drive him out between the lines, so he can see who he's about to fight. He looks across. Grandfathers. Teachers. Uncles, cousins, sons, friends. His own family, standing in both armies, and many of them on the other side. His mouth goes dry, the bow slips from his hand, and he sinks down onto the seat of his chariot. He says he can't do this. His freeze comes on a battlefield. The same kind of freeze can come anywhere: in a hallway, outside a door nobody wants to open. That moment is where the Bhagavad Gita begins. And the word Arjuna reaches for, to say what he's lost, is today's word.
screen: `TWO ARMIES.` → `HIS OWN FAMILY, ACROSS THE FIELD.` → `THE BOW SLIPS.`

segments.voice: Dharma. In English it gets translated as duty, or law, or religion, and each of those catches only a piece. The Sanskrit comes from a root meaning to hold, to support. Dharma is what holds things up. Teachers sometimes put it this way: the dharma of fire is to burn, the dharma of water is to flow. It's what a thing is for, the part it holds in the whole. Now back to the chariot. Arjuna turns to his driver, who is Krishna, and who turns out to be a great deal more than a driver. And Arjuna says, in the second chapter of the Gita, that his mind is confused about dharma. He doesn't know what's right anymore. Then he says something brave: I am your student. Teach me. The rest of the Gita is that teaching, and we'll come back to it on this path. For today, hold one line from the third chapter. Krishna says it's better to do your own dharma, even imperfectly, than someone else's dharma done well. Your own. The Sanskrit is svadharma. So dharma isn't only a rulebook handed down from above. It's also a question you can ask about your own life, today: what is mine to do here? Not what's easiest. Not what someone else should be doing. Mine. Notice that Arjuna isn't lacking information. He knows exactly who's on that field. What he's lost is the thread of what's his to do. That's the thread the Gita hands back.
screen: `DHARMA — WHAT HOLDS THINGS UP.` · `I AM YOUR STUDENT. TEACH ME.` · `YOUR OWN, EVEN IMPERFECTLY.` · then, large: `WHAT IS MINE TO DO HERE?`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first breath, let one small place come to mind where you're a little frozen. Not the biggest thing. A message you haven't answered, a thing you said you'd do. On the second breath, ask it, silently, once: what's mine to do here? On the third, let the question rest. No plan. Just breathe out.
Dharma. From a root meaning to hold. What holds things up, and your own share of the holding. Third word.

Your line: do the thing that's yours to do. Pick the small frozen one from the practice and do one piece of it today. One reply, one step. If someone's with you, ask each other the same question: what's mine to do here? That's day three.

screen: `DAY 3 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHY IT'S SAID THREE TIMES.`

howItsDone: Hindus speak of dharma as right action and the order that holds life together, and also of svadharma, one's own duty in a given place and stage of life; the Bhagavad Gita is read and recited as a guide to it.

fork.setup: you're Arjuna. your family is across the field, your bow is on the floor of the chariot, and you don't know what's right. what do you do?
options: order the chariot off the field.
tell your charioteer you're his student, and ask him to teach you.
pick up the bow without a word.
fork.reveal: Arjuna says his mind is confused about dharma and asks Krishna to teach him. the whole Bhagavad Gita is the answer.

original.note: Sanskrit, from the root dhṛ: to hold, to support.

trapdoor: what you thought: duty, or rules.
what it means: what holds things up, and the part that's yours to hold.
what a scholar hears: from dhṛ, to hold; Gita 2.7 has Arjuna confused about dharma, and Gita 3.35 prefers one's own dharma, imperfect, to another's done well.

story.title: the dog at heaven's gate
story.text: At the very end of the Mahabharata, the five Pandava brothers and Draupadi walk toward the Himalayas, and one by one they fall. Only the eldest, Yudhishthira, is left, with a dog that has followed him the whole way. The god Indra arrives in a chariot to carry him to heaven, but says the dog can't come. Yudhishthira refuses. He won't abandon someone who stayed loyal to him, not even for heaven. Then the dog changes shape. It was Dharma himself, testing him, and Yudhishthira had passed.

wrong.truth: it's wider. from a root meaning to hold, it's what holds things up, including the part that's yours to hold.

Gita 2.7 (dharma-sammudha-chetah, 'I am your disciple, teach me') and 3.35 (svadharma) paraphrased; confirm.
